steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Astrophotography records images of celestial objects using cameras attached to telescopes or with standard cameras on tripods

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Key camera settings: exposure time, ISO/gain, and aperture (f-number)

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Star trails are created by long exposures showing the apparent rotation of the sky around the celestial pole

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Image stacking combines multiple short exposures to reduce noise and reveal faint detail

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Q: What is image stacking and why is it used? | Q: What are dark frames and flat frames? | Q: How are star trail images created?

steps.title: Check your answers
steps.body: Combining multiple short exposures of the same object to reduce random noise and increase signal-to-noise ratio, revealing fainter detail than a single long exposure. | Dark frames: exposures with the lens cap on, recording sensor noise for subtraction. Flat frames: images of a uniform light source, correcting vignetting and dust shadows on the sensor. | By taking a very long exposure (or stacking many short ones) while the camera remains fixed, recording the apparent circular motion of stars around the celestial pole.

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Stacking improves signal-to-noise ratio — this is a key concept Dark frames subtract noise; flat frames correct vignetting — know the difference Both boards cover astrophotography basics in the observational skills section The 500 rule is useful but not always examined — understand the principle rather than memorising the number
